title: “THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS LIKE EAGLES” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING GOD’S PROMISE ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: “THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS LIKE EAGLES” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING GOD’S PROMISE ALL ALONG?

Isaiah 40:31 was never mainly about becoming successful, achieving your dreams, or rising above everyone else. It was spoken to exhausted people who wondered whether God had forgotten them. And once you understand what God was actually promising, you may never read this verse the same way again.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You wake up tired. You smile because people expect you to. You answer, “I’m okay,” because explaining what is happening inside your heart would take more strength than you have left.
You still believe in God.
You still pray.
You still open your Bible, even if some days you stare at the words without feeling anything.

But somewhere between the prayers that seem unanswered, the responsibilities that never stop, the disappointments you never expected, and the battles nobody knows you are fighting, a question has quietly settled into your soul.
Lord, how much longer can I keep going?
And perhaps the hardest part is that you have heard Christians quote Isaiah 40:31 countless times.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”

You have seen those words printed beneath pictures of majestic birds flying over mountains. You have heard them preached as encouragement to dream bigger, reach higher, break limitations, and achieve extraordinary things.
And perhaps you have wondered why, if God promised you wings, you still feel like you are crawling.
Why does everyone else seem to be soaring while you are struggling just to survive?
Why does the person who barely acknowledges God appear to be prospering while you, who have been trying to remain faithful, can hardly catch your breath?
What if the problem is not that God has failed to fulfill His promise?
What if we have been asking this promise to mean something God never intended it to mean?
Because Isaiah 40:31 is not primarily a motivational speech for ambitious people.
It is a divine word of comfort for weary people.
And to understand its beauty, we must return to the people who first received it.
Before God spoke about eagle's wings, He spoke to people who believed their suffering had become invisible to Him.
Listen to the complaint recorded in Isaiah 40:27:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?” (KJV)
Do you hear the heartbreak?
God's people were not simply asking how to become more successful.
They were asking whether God still saw them.
Their circumstances had become so painful that they began to wonder whether their lives mattered to the One who had made a covenant with them.

Isaiah 40 speaks comfort into the shadow of exile. The preceding chapter announces the coming Babylonian crisis, while Isaiah 40 addresses God's people with hope beyond judgment, anticipating their restoration.
Jerusalem would suffer. The people would experience displacement and humiliation. Their national security, religious confidence, and familiar way of life would be shaken.
And beneath their suffering was a terrifying question.
Has the God who chose us abandoned us?
Perhaps you have never experienced exile from your homeland.
But you may know what it feels like to become a stranger to the life you once recognized.
You had plans.
You thought your marriage would be different.
You thought your family would remain together.
You thought the business would survive.
You thought the diagnosis would be better.
You thought the person you trusted would never betray you.
You thought that by this stage of your life, you would be somewhere else.
Instead, you find yourself standing among the ruins of expectations you once carried with confidence.
And although you would never say it publicly, sometimes your prayers sound painfully similar to Israel's complaint.
God, have You overlooked me?
This is where the promise of eagle's wings begins.
Not with achievement.
With abandonment fears.
Not with a guarantee of prosperity.
With God's answer to people who believe they have been forgotten.
And His answer is more magnificent than a promise to make them rich, famous, influential, or admired.
He reminds them who He is.
Isaiah 40:28 declares:
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.” (KJV)
Notice what God does not say.
He does not tell His people that their suffering is imaginary.
He does not accuse them of being worthless because they are exhausted.
He does not promise that their circumstances will immediately become comfortable.
He directs their attention away from the limits of their strength and toward the limitless strength of their Creator.
The God who made the ends of the earth does not become exhausted.
The God who governs history does not run out of wisdom.
The God who sustains creation does not lose track of His people.
And that means something extraordinary.
Your strength may be running out, but God's strength is not.
There is a difference between those two realities, and confusing them has wounded many sincere believers.
Some Christians have been taught to treat exhaustion as proof of spiritual failure.
If you were really faithful, you would never feel overwhelmed.
If you prayed enough, you would never struggle.
If your faith were strong enough, you would always be victorious, energetic, confident, and emotionally unshakable.
But that is not what Isaiah says.
In fact, Isaiah 40:29 declares:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.” (KJV)
Read that again.
He gives power to the faint.
Not merely to the impressive.
Not only to the influential.
Not exclusively to those whose lives look victorious.
To the faint.
The Hebrew word translated “faint” here comes from יָעֵף (yaʿef), associated with being weary or exhausted.
God knows what weariness is.
He knows the difference between rebellion and human limitation.
He knows when His children are carrying burdens they cannot sustain by their own power.
And His promise is not that genuine believers will never become weak.
His promise is that He is able to strengthen those who are weak.
That distinction matters.
Because some of you have been ashamed of the very weakness that should have driven you toward the Lord.
You have been pretending to be strong because you thought weakness would disappoint Him.
You have been hiding your tears because you assumed mature Christians were supposed to have everything under control.
You have been measuring your spiritual life by how productive, cheerful, successful, and emotionally stable you appear.
But Isaiah does not tell exhausted people to manufacture an impressive appearance.
He tells them to look to the everlasting God.
And then comes the verse so many of us have memorized.
Isaiah 40:31:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.” (KJV)
Beautiful.
Familiar.
Often quoted.
But the meaning becomes even richer when we examine the Hebrew.
The expression translated “wait upon the LORD” is:
וְקוֹיֵ יְהוָה — veqovey YHWH
It refers to those who wait for, hope in, or look expectantly to the LORD.
The verb is related to the Hebrew root קוה (q-w-h), commonly associated with waiting and hoping.
This is not simply waiting for circumstances to improve while doing nothing.
Nor is it a formula for forcing God to deliver whatever outcome we desire.
It is expectant dependence upon the LORD Himself.
It is the posture of someone who says:
God, I do not understand everything You are doing, but I will not abandon my hope in You.
I cannot see the entire road, but I will trust the One who can.
I do not possess enough strength for everything ahead, but I believe You remain faithful.
This kind of waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is trust that continues when immediate answers do not come.
It is obedience when obedience is costly.
It is prayer when words are difficult.
It is refusing to make despair the final authority over your life.
And sometimes it looks remarkably ordinary.
Getting out of bed.
Opening Scripture.
Asking forgiveness.
Choosing not to retaliate.
Showing up for your family.
Seeking help when the burden becomes too heavy.
Taking the next faithful step without knowing how the entire journey will unfold.
That may not look like soaring.
But heaven does not measure faithfulness by how impressive it appears to other people.
Now consider another Hebrew expression:
יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ — yaḥalifu koaḥ
The phrase is translated in the KJV as “shall renew their strength.”
The verb comes from חלף (ḥ-l-f), which can carry the sense of changing, replacing, or renewing, depending on its context.
Here, the idea is that those who hope in the LORD receive renewed strength.
It is not a promise that human beings become limitless.
It is not a guarantee that every faithful person will possess extraordinary physical energy.
It is not a declaration that Christians will never experience illness, emotional distress, financial hardship, or suffering.
It is God's assurance that His people are not ultimately left to depend upon their own inadequate resources.
The strength they need comes from Him.
And this is where the eagle imagery becomes so powerful.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”
The Hebrew expression is:
יַעֲלוּ אֵבֶר כַּנְּשָׁרִים — yaʿalu ever kannešarim
The image is of rising or ascending with wings like eagles.
The Hebrew word נֶשֶׁר (nešer) refers to a great bird of prey, often translated “eagle,” though its usage may include birds such as vultures in some contexts.
The image communicates remarkable strength and elevation.
But we must be careful not to build doctrines upon popular stories about eagles that Scripture itself never teaches.
You may have heard claims that an eagle must break off its beak, remove its talons, or pluck out its feathers to be reborn into a stronger life.
Those dramatic stories are not reliable descriptions of eagle biology.
And Isaiah does not teach them.
The power of God's Word does not need a fabricated nature story to make it more inspiring.
The image is already glorious.
God promises renewed strength to those who wait upon Him.
And notice something that often disappears when this verse becomes a slogan about success.
The promise does not end with flying.
It continues:
“They shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.”
Flying.
Running.
Walking.
Three images.
One divine assurance.
God is able to sustain His people.
And perhaps the final image is the one some of us need most.
Because sometimes the greatest evidence of God's sustaining grace is not that you are flying above your problems. It is that you are still walking with Him through them.
Think about that.
There are seasons when life seems full of extraordinary spiritual encouragement.
You feel energized.
You see answers to prayer.
Doors open.
Your heart overflows with gratitude.
You feel as though you could run for miles.
But there are other seasons.
Seasons when you have to fight just to remain faithful.
When you cannot see the next breakthrough.
When the same temptation returns.
When grief interrupts ordinary moments.
When you are caring for someone who cannot care for themselves.
When the bills are waiting.
When the marriage requires another difficult conversation.
When the children need patience you barely have.
When your body hurts.
When your mind is overwhelmed.
When your prayers are shorter because your tears are longer.
And you wonder whether God is disappointed that you are no longer soaring.
But the promise includes walking.
Not every season will feel spectacular.
Not every victory will attract attention.
Not every act of faithfulness will produce a dramatic testimony that thousands of people share.
Sometimes faithfulness is simply continuing to trust God when the road is long.
And that is not insignificant.
It is precious.
Yet we must go even deeper.
Because Isaiah 40:31 is not an isolated promise floating in a collection of inspirational sayings.
It belongs to the larger story of God's redemption.
Isaiah 40 begins with words of extraordinary tenderness:
“Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.” (Isaiah 40:1, KJV)
The chapter announces comfort for God's people and speaks of the LORD coming to rescue and restore.
Then Isaiah 40:3 declares:
“The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.” (KJV)
Centuries later, the New Testament identifies John the Baptist's ministry with this wilderness proclamation.
Matthew 3:3 explicitly connects John's message to Isaiah's words.
John came preparing the way for Jesus Christ.
And suddenly the horizon becomes even greater.
The God who promised comfort to weary Israel was unfolding a redemptive plan that would reach its fulfillment in Jesus.
The New Testament does not reduce Isaiah's original message to a prediction of personal success.
It shows that God's promised salvation reaches its climactic revelation in Christ.
And here is something that should stop us in our tracks.
The One who gives strength to the weary entered our weary world and experienced genuine human exhaustion.
John 4:6 tells us that Jesus, wearied by His journey, sat beside Jacob's well.
The eternal Son of God truly became human.
He knew hunger.
He knew thirst.
He knew grief.
He knew what it meant to be rejected.
He knew the pain of betrayal.
He knew the weight of sorrow.
And in the Garden of Gethsemane, He faced suffering of a depth we cannot fully comprehend.
Jesus did not come into this world merely to teach exhausted people how to become more productive.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins upon the cross.
He came to defeat death through His resurrection.
He came to accomplish what no amount of human determination, ambition, or religious performance could ever accomplish.
Our redemption.
And this is where the Gospel confronts a misunderstanding that can quietly poison the Christian life.
We sometimes approach God as though Christianity were a transaction.
We give Him our prayers, our service, our offerings, and our obedience.
And in return, we expect uninterrupted success.
We assume that faithfulness should guarantee financial abundance, physical health, public recognition, and protection from disappointment.
But the cross tells a different story.
The perfectly obedient Son of God suffered.
The sinless Savior was rejected.
The Lord of glory was crucified.
And His suffering was not evidence that the Father had lost control.
It was central to God's saving purpose.
If our definition of divine favor cannot make sense of the cross, our definition needs to change.
Because Jesus did not redeem us by avoiding suffering.
He redeemed us through His obedient suffering, death, and victorious resurrection.
That does not mean every tragedy has an explanation we can identify.
It does not mean suffering is good in itself.
It does not mean Christians should remain in abusive situations, neglect medical care, or refuse necessary help because they believe endurance requires silence.
It means suffering cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence that God has abandoned His children.
And that truth changes how we read Isaiah 40:31.
The promise of renewed strength is not permission to worship achievement.
It is an invitation to depend upon the God who saves.
And Jesus gives that invitation a deeply personal voice.
In Matthew 11:28, He says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
In the Greek New Testament, the invitation begins:
Δεῦτε πρός με — Deute pros me
“Come to me.”
Not merely, “Come to a better strategy.”
Not, “Come to a more successful version of yourself.”
Not, “Come once you have fixed your life.”
Come to Me.
The word translated “heavy laden” is πεφορτισμένοι (pephortismenoi), describing those who have been burdened or loaded down.
Jesus is addressing the weary and burdened, offering rest under His gracious lordship.
He does not invite us to a life without obedience.
In the following verses, He calls us to take His yoke and learn from Him.
But His yoke is not the crushing burden of trying to earn acceptance before God through our own righteousness.
He is gentle and lowly in heart.
He offers rest for our souls.
And that rest is not merely the relief of getting everything we want.
It is the blessing of belonging to Him.
Perhaps that is what you have been missing.
You have been asking Jesus to give you wings so you can escape your circumstances.
But He is calling you to Himself so you can learn to trust Him in every circumstance.
You have been praying for enough success to finally feel secure.
But your deepest security is not found in your achievements.
It is found in the Savior who gave Himself for you.
You have been asking God to prove His love by making your road easier.
But the greatest demonstration of His love has already been revealed at Calvary.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we achieved financial stability.
Not after we developed a perfect reputation.
Not after we conquered every weakness.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
This is grace.
And grace is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe your story contains things you wish you could erase.
A relationship you destroyed.
A lie you told.
A habit you kept hidden.
A season of rebellion.
A betrayal.
A secret sin.
A decision that still makes you uncomfortable when you remember it.
Maybe people know your worst chapter and have decided it is the only chapter worth remembering.
Maybe you have even begun to believe them.
But the Gospel announces something astonishing.
Your sin is serious.
Your need for repentance is real.
And the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than your ability to save yourself.
He does not offer forgiveness by pretending sin does not matter.
He bore sin's judgment at the cross.
He does not call us to repentance because He enjoys humiliating broken people.
He calls us to turn from sin and trust Him because life is found in Him.
The grace that forgives also begins to transform.
And the Christ who receives repentant sinners does not leave them without hope.
From scandal to grace is not the story of people who finally became good enough for God. It is the story of a Savior whose mercy reaches people who could never rescue themselves.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted that even if others abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denials.
Three times Peter denied knowing the Lord.
And when the rooster crowed, his failure became unbearable.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The man who had walked with Jesus.
The man who had witnessed miracles.
The man who had spoken boldly about faithfulness.
Now broken by the memory of his own words.
If Peter's story ended there, it would be a devastating account of human failure.
But it did not end there.
The risen Jesus restored Peter, as recorded in John 21.
He confronted him with love, called him again to shepherd His sheep, and gave him a future of faithful service.
Peter's restoration did not erase the seriousness of his denial.
It demonstrated the mercy and authority of the risen Christ.
That is the Gospel's power.
Not that our failures are harmless.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Not that every earthly consequence disappears.
But that Jesus Christ is able to forgive, restore, and transform those who return to Him.
Perhaps you are reading this with a heart that feels more like Peter's courtyard than an eagle soaring over mountains.
You remember what you promised God.
You remember what you did instead.
You remember the compromises.
The excuses.
The moments when fear mattered more to you than faithfulness.
And you wonder whether you have disqualified yourself from ever being useful again.
Do not confuse conviction with a declaration that Christ cannot forgive you.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing sin, do not hide it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
Receive the mercy that is found in Jesus.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
The answer to spiritual failure is not pretending you never fell.
It is returning to the Savior who died and rose again.
And perhaps your greatest need today is not another motivational message about reaching the top.
Perhaps you need to kneel before the Lord and say:
Jesus, I have spent so much time trying to build a life that looks successful that I have neglected the life of faithfulness You are calling me to live.
I have compared myself to others.
I have confused comfort with blessing.
I have treated unanswered prayers as evidence that You do not care.
I have tried to appear strong while my soul was becoming exhausted.
Forgive me.
Teach me to wait upon You.
Teach me to trust You.
Teach me to walk with You, even when I cannot see the road ahead.
And if those words expose something you have been carrying, you do not have to pretend otherwise.
You can be honest before God.
You can be honest with a trusted brother or sister in Christ.
Not to prove your faith to strangers.
Not because typing a phrase earns God's favor.
But because sometimes an honest confession becomes the beginning of a conversation another weary believer desperately needs.
Someone else may read your words and realize they are not the only person struggling to trust God.
Someone may find courage to admit that their own spiritual life has become exhausted.
The Christian life was never intended to be lived entirely alone.
We need the Word.
We need prayer.
We need the fellowship of believers.
We need the local church.
We need brothers and sisters who will tell us the truth with love.
And above all, we need Christ.
Because there is another danger hidden inside the popular interpretation of Isaiah 40:31.
When we turn eagle's wings into a guarantee of worldly success, we can unintentionally make struggling believers feel condemned.
The business owner whose company failed may wonder whether he lacked faith.
The mother whose child remains seriously ill may wonder whether she prayed incorrectly.
The faithful worker who never receives a promotion may wonder whether God favors everyone else.
The believer living with chronic pain may wonder whether the promise of renewed strength somehow excludes them.
But Isaiah 40:31 is not a weapon to use against the weary.
It is a word of hope for them.
And the New Testament confirms that God's sustaining grace does not always appear as the removal of weakness.
The apostle Paul pleaded with the Lord concerning a painful affliction he called a thorn in the flesh.
The Lord's answer was not immediate removal.
In 2 Corinthians 12:9, Jesus told him:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” (KJV)
Paul did not conclude that God's grace had failed because the affliction remained.
He learned to depend more deeply upon Christ.
That is not a command to enjoy suffering.
It is an assurance that weakness does not place us beyond the reach of divine grace.
And one day, God's people will experience a restoration far greater than anything this present world can offer.
The resurrection of Jesus guarantees that death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The Christian hope is not limited to improved circumstances before we die.
It reaches toward the resurrection, the renewal of creation, and eternal fellowship with God.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
That future is not a reward for people who achieved the most impressive earthly success.
It is the inheritance of those redeemed by the Lamb.
So yes, God may open doors for you.
He may bless your work.
He may grant healing.
He may restore relationships.
He may provide opportunities beyond anything you imagined.
Receive such gifts with gratitude.
But do not make them the foundation of your faith.
Because if your confidence in God depends entirely upon favorable circumstances, every storm will threaten to destroy it.
Build your hope upon Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who remains faithful when circumstances change.
The One who is worthy of worship when prayers are answered as we hoped, and still worthy when the answers are difficult to understand.
The One who holds His people even when their hands are trembling.
And now, perhaps, we can hear Isaiah 40:31 differently.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”
Not necessarily because they will become famous.
Not because they will always have money.
Not because they will never suffer.
Not because everyone who opposes them will watch them achieve spectacular success.
But because the everlasting God is able to renew and sustain those who place their hope in Him.
“They shall run, and not be weary.”
Not because human strength is infinite.
But because God's power is not exhausted.
“And they shall walk, and not faint.”
Even when the road is long.
Even when progress is slow.
Even when the next step requires courage.
Even when nobody applauds.
Even when the testimony is still being written.
And perhaps this is the part that makes the promise so deeply personal.
You may not be where you expected to be.
You may still be waiting for an answer.
You may still be grieving.
You may still be recovering from something that changed your life.
You may still be learning how to pray again after a season of disappointment.
You may be carrying responsibilities that seem heavier every morning.
But your present exhaustion does not mean that God has ceased to be faithful.
You are not required to manufacture the strength of the everlasting God.
You are invited to trust Him.
And sometimes that trust will feel courageous.
Sometimes it will feel quiet.
Sometimes it will look like worship.
Sometimes it will look like repentance.
Sometimes it will look like reaching out for help.
Sometimes it will look like taking one more step in obedience to Christ.
Do not despise that step.
The world celebrates people who appear to be soaring.
But the Lord sees the believer who keeps walking with Him when the journey is painful.
And He knows every tear.
He knows every prayer.
He knows every act of obedience that nobody else notices.
He knows the burdens you have never found words to explain.
And His invitation remains:
Come to Christ.
Hope in the LORD.
Receive His grace.
Walk in His truth.
And keep your eyes fixed upon the Savior who has already conquered sin and death.
If this message has helped you understand Isaiah 40:31 more faithfully, consider saving it.

Not because every difficult day can be solved by rereading an article, but because the Scriptures explored here may help you return your attention to Christ when weariness begins to distort your perspective.
There may be someone among your family, friends, or acquaintances who has been silently wondering whether God has forgotten them.
They may never tell you what they are going through.
But a Scripture-centered message shared at the right moment can open a door to encouragement, prayer, and a deeper conversation about Jesus.
Not to put their private struggles on display.
Simply to remind them that the Christian hope is greater than the pressure to appear successful.
And if you know someone who has drifted from faith, or someone who has never understood the Gospel, invite them to read and consider the claims of Jesus for themselves.
We are not trying to gather people around a personality.
We want to direct hearts toward Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your Bible.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to replace faithful pastors, Christian fellowship, or personal discipleship.
But to serve as another place where people can encounter Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, calls to repentance, and reminders of the grace of Jesus Christ.
A friend who is exhausted.
A family member who is searching.
A believer who needs encouragement.
Someone who has been wounded by shallow teaching.
Someone who needs to hear that Christianity is not a promise of effortless success, but the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ.
And if you want to help us continue and expand this work, I want to speak to you about something important.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
But Scripture also teaches that believers may voluntarily support those who labor in Gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.
But it is not a spiritual obligation, a replacement for faithful giving to your local church, or a requirement for glorifying God.
You are no less welcome here.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still invite someone to read Scripture.
You can still encourage a struggling believer.
Your worth before God has never depended upon your ability to give money.
These products are not the reason to follow Jesus, and they do not make anyone more spiritual.
They are simply a tangible expression of appreciation for those who choose to help sustain the work.

These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, develop habits of prayer and discipleship, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
The library's free resources remain a way for people to learn and grow without making financial support a condition of access.
A thoughtful comment may begin a conversation about faith.
A personal invitation may encourage someone to return to prayer, seek Christian fellowship, or open the Bible again.
The goal is that more people would come to know, love, trust, and follow Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, I want to return to the question that began this conversation.
What if you have been wondering why God promised you eagle's wings when you can barely walk?
What if the verse was never meant to shame you for not flying high enough?
What if it was meant to remind you that the everlasting God has not exhausted His strength?
What if you have been measuring your life by the height of your achievements while God has been calling you to the depth of your trust?
What if the most important thing about your story is not whether the world considers you successful?
What if the most important thing is whether you belong to Jesus Christ?
Because one day, the applause will stop.
The achievements will fade.
The possessions will pass away.
The titles will no longer matter.
The numbers on our screens will mean nothing.
But the salvation accomplished by Jesus Christ will remain.
And those who belong to Him will discover that their hope was never misplaced.
So if you are tired tonight, come to Him.
If you have sinned, repent and seek His forgiveness.
If you are grieving, bring Him your sorrow.
If you are confused, seek His wisdom in Scripture.
If you are struggling, do not be ashamed to ask for prayer and help.
If you are waiting, do not assume waiting means you have been abandoned.
And if all you can do today is take one faithful step, take it with your eyes upon Christ.
You do not need to impress Him with a performance of strength.
You need the grace of the Savior.
Are you in a season of soaring, running, or simply trying to keep walking with God?
You can share your testimony, your struggle, a prayer request, or simply write “I'm still walking with Jesus.”
There is no need to disclose anything you would rather keep private.
But perhaps your honest words will encourage another believer who has been quietly wondering whether they are the only one still struggling.
Because Isaiah 40:31 was never mainly about how high you could rise in the eyes of the world.
It was about the faithfulness of the God who gives strength to the weary.
And the greatest gift He has given us is not worldly success.
It is His Son.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling the weary to Himself.
Worthy of our trust.
Worthy of our repentance.
Worthy of our worship.
Worthy of our lives.
And when the world sees only how slowly you are walking, remember this: the Savior who carried your sin to the cross has not stopped being faithful to you on the road.
